content:
Every December, the Christmas card shows one scene: a stable, a manger, shepherds and three kings kneeling side by side. Muslims are often told that the Quran tells the same story, or that it tells a garbled copy of it. Both claims compare the Quran with the card, and the card is neither Matthew nor Luke.

The Quran and the two Gospels agree on the heart of the event. Mary conceived Jesus (peace be upon him) without a man, by the will of God: "She said: 'O my Lord! How shall I have a son when no man hath touched me?' He said: 'Even so: Allah createth what He willeth'" (3:47).[1] Around that agreement the three accounts are built differently.

This article aims to provide context to the comparison, insha'Allah, in five differences between Surah Maryam, Matthew and Luke, read in their own words. We set out the Quranic passage verse by verse in the birth of Jesus in Surah Maryam.

In Luke, the angel Gabriel comes to Mary in Nazareth: "Behold, you will conceive in your womb, and give birth to a son, and will call his name 'Jesus'" (Luke 1:31).[2] In Matthew, Mary is already with child when the story begins, and the angel speaks to Joseph in a dream: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 1:20).[2]

The Quran gives the news to Mary alone, twice. In Surah Al ʿImran the angels say: "O Mary! Allah giveth thee glad tidings of a Word from Him: his name will be Christ Jesus, the son of Mary" (3:45). In Surah Maryam God's messenger appears to her "as a man in all respects" (19:17).[1] Joseph does not appear in the Quran at all.

Luke names Bethlehem and a census, and gives one sentence to the birth: "She wrapped him in bands of cloth, and laid him in a feeding trough, because there was no room for them in the inn" (Luke 2:7). Matthew names Bethlehem and says nothing of the birth itself; by the time the wise men arrive, the family is in "the house" (Matthew 2:11).[2]

The Quran names no town. It gives the birth more space than either Gospel: "And the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm-tree: She cried (in her anguish): 'Ah! would that I had died before this!'" (19:23). A voice answers her with water and "fresh ripe dates" (19:24 to 25).[1] There is no manger and no inn.

Some Muslim writers read the ripe dates as proof of a summer birth. The verse gives provision to Mary, and the Quran has already said that God provided for her "without measure" (3:37).[1] We set out what can be known of the date in was Jesus born on 25 December?

Luke brings shepherds "staying in the field, and keeping watch by night over their flock" (Luke 2:8), told by an angel: "For there is born to you today, in David's city, a Savior, who is Christ the Lord" (Luke 2:11).[2] Matthew brings "wise men from the east" to Herod's Jerusalem (Matthew 2:1), and the visit leads to the killing of the children of Bethlehem and the flight into Egypt.[2]

The Gospels never put the two visits together. Matthew never says there were three wise men; the number came later, from the three gifts of "gold, frankincense, and myrrh" (Matthew 2:11).[2]

The Quran has neither shepherds nor wise men. The witnesses are Mary's own people, and they come to accuse her: "O Mary! truly an amazing thing hast thou brought! O sister of Aaron! Thy father was not a man of evil, nor thy mother a woman unchaste!" (19:27 to 28).[1]

Mary, under a vow of silence, points to the child. Her people ask: "How can we talk to one who is a child in the cradle?" (19:29). The infant answers: "I am indeed a servant of Allah: He hath given me revelation and made me a prophet; And He hath made me blessed wheresoever I be, and hath enjoined on me Prayer and Charity as long as I live" (19:30 to 31).[1]

Neither Matthew nor Luke has any words from the infant Jesus. The first words Luke gives him come at the age of twelve, in the Temple, "sitting in the middle of the teachers, both listening to them, and asking them questions" (Luke 2:46).[2] In the Quran, the speech in the cradle clears his mother's name, and its first word about himself is "servant".

Matthew reads the birth through Isaiah: "They shall call his name Immanuel; which is, being interpreted, 'God with us'" (Matthew 1:23). Luke's angel says the child "will be called the Son of God" (Luke 1:35).[2] Christian theology reads these lines with the rest of the New Testament, and with the creeds, as the beginning of the incarnation.

The Quran gives the meaning in the same passage as the birth: "Such (was) Jesus the son of Mary: (it is) a statement of truth, about which they (vainly) dispute" (19:34). The child's own speech ends in the call to worship: "Verily Allah is my Lord and your Lord: Him therefore serve ye: this is a Way that is straight" (19:36).[1] The miracle is a sign of God's power to create, as Adam was (3:59). We set out that answer in full in does the virgin birth make Jesus divine?

The bottom line

Surah Maryam, Matthew and Luke agree on the miracle: Mary conceived her son without a man, by God's command. They differ on who heard the news, where the child was born, who came to see him, whether he spoke, and what the birth means. The Christmas card merges Matthew and Luke into one scene. The Quran tells a third account, in its own words and with its own meaning.

The Quran's account ends where its meaning lies, with the child's words: "I am indeed a servant of Allah" (19:30).[1] Muslims honour the birth of Jesus as the birth of a prophet, in the words he himself is given in the cradle. Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Quran 3:37; 3:45 to 47; 3:59; 19:16 to 36, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  2. Matthew 1:18 to 2:23; Luke 1:26 to 2:52 (World English Bible).
